title: Safari (web browser)
wiki_lead:
Safari is a web browser developed by Apple. It is built into several of Apple's operating systems, including macOS, iOS, iPadOS, and visionOS, and uses Apple's open-source browser engine WebKit, which was derived from KHTML. It is the second most used browser in the world, after Google Chrome.
Safari was introduced in an update to Mac OS X Jaguar in January 2003, and made the default web browser with the release of Mac OS X Panther that same year, replacing Internet Explorer for Mac. It has been included with the iPhone since the first-generation iPhone in 2007. At that time, Safari was the fastest browser on the Mac. Between 2007 and 2012, Apple maintained a Windows version, but abandoned it due to low market share. In 2010, Safari 5 introduced a reader mode, extensions, and developer tools. Safari 11, released in 2017, added Intelligent Tracking Prevention, which uses artificial intelligence to block web tracking. Safari 13 added support for Apple Pay, and authentication with FIDO2 security keys. Its user interface was redesigned in Safari 15, Safari 18, and Safari 26.

History and development


Background
Netscape Navigator rapidly became the dominant Mac browser after its 1994 release, and eventually came bundled with Mac OS. In 1996, Microsoft released Internet Explorer for Mac (IE), and Apple released the Cyberdog internet suite, which included a web browser. In 1997, Apple shelved Cyberdog and reached a five-year agreement with Microsoft to make IE the default browser on the Mac, starting with Mac OS 8.1. Netscape continued to be preinstalled on all Macintosh systems. Microsoft continued to update IE for Mac, which was ported to Mac OS X DP4 in May 2000.


Conception
Apple introduced the Safari web browser on January 7, 2003. At the time, Steve Jobs called Safari "a turbo browser for Mac OS X". Apple created Safari for speed, calling it the fastest browser for the Mac. Jobs compared it with Internet Explorer, Netscape, and Chimera (later renamed Camino), and demonstrated that Safari's speed was faster. The second reason that Apple created Safari was to innovate; Apple wanted to make a browser better than their competitors. During development, several codenames were used, including "Freedom", "iBrowse", and "Alexander" (a reference to conqueror Alexander the Great, an homage to the Konqueror web browser).


Safari 1
On January 7, 2003, at Macworld San Francisco, Apple CEO Steve Jobs announced Safari that was based on WebKit, the company's internal fork of the KHTML browser engine. Apple released the first beta version exclusively on Mac OS X the same day. After that date, several official and unofficial beta versions followed until version 1.0 was released on June 23, 2003. On Mac OS X v10.3, Safari was pre-installed as the system's default browser, rather than requiring a manual download, as was the case with the previous Mac OS X versions. Safari's predecessor, the Internet Explorer for Mac, was then included in 10.3 as an alternative.
grok_lead: Safari is a graphical web browser developed by Apple Inc., first released as a public beta on December 13, 2002, and officially as version 1.0 on June 23, 2003, serving as the default browser for macOS and later iOS, iPadOS, and other Apple platforms. Built upon the open-source WebKit rendering engine, which Apple co-developed from KHTML, Safari prioritizes seamless integration within the Apple ecosystem, including iCloud synchronization of tabs, bookmarks, and passwords across devices. Safari distinguishes itself through hardware-optimized performance on Apple silicon, yielding superior battery life and JavaScript execution speeds in controlled benchmarks compared to competitors like Google Chrome on equivalent hardware. Its core defining characteristic is an emphasis on user privacy, featuring built-in tools such as Intelligent Tracking Prevention, which employs machine learning to detect and block cross-site trackers, and Private Browsing mode that avoids storing history or cookies. These protections extend to fingerprinting resistance and IP address hiding from trackers, activated by default without user intervention. As of 2025, Safari commands approximately 16-17% of the global desktop and mobile browser market share, with higher penetration on iOS devices due to its pre-installation and App Store policies limiting alternatives until recent EU regulatory changes. Notable achievements include pioneering top-site thumbnails and reader mode for ad-free viewing, while controversies arise from its WebKit exclusivity on iOS âcriticized for stifling engine diversity and innovationâand occasional compatibility issues with non-standard web content optimized for Chromium-based browsers. Despite these, empirical tests affirm Safari's causal edge in resource efficiency, reducing power draw by up to 50% over rivals on macOS, underscoring its design rationale tied to Apple's closed hardware-software integration.
